say: That fluffy cloud floating over your house weighs about one point one million pounds. So why isn't it falling on your head?
Picture a normal puffy cumulus cloud. Scientists model it as a giant box, about one kilometer on every side.
Every cubic meter of that cloud holds only about half a gram of liquid water. Way less than a teaspoon!
But that box holds a billion cubic meters. That adds up to five hundred thousand kilograms, about as heavy as a hundred elephants!
The trick is size. Cloud droplets are only a few thousandths of a millimeter across, smaller than the width of a human hair.
Droplets that tiny fall ridiculously slowly, about eighteen to thirty six meters an hour. You could out-walk one.
Meanwhile, warm air keeps rising from below, and those updrafts push the droplets up faster than they can sink.
And here's the wild part. The air inside that same box weighs about a billion kilograms. The water is just a tiny passenger.
So when does it rain? When about a million droplets crash together into one raindrop, finally heavy enough to fall.
So yes, there's a herd of elephants floating above you. Follow Simply Weird for more weird stuff like this.
